Excellent report — the repro file did most of the work. Two findings, and they split cleanly.

**The thickness is our bug, and it's a one-liner.** The converter parses your 0.15 m depth correctly and then throws it away. In `packages/ifc-converter/src/index.ts` the slab node is built with the thickness stuffed into `metadata` under this comment:

```
// to metadata so the IFC value isn't lost.
```

That comment is simply out of date — `SlabNode` has had `thickness: z.number().default(0.05)` for a while. So the field falls back to 0.05 m, which is **0.164 ft** — your 0.16 ft, exactly. Fixing this is passing one value through and deleting a stale comment.

**The offset is your exporter, and your hypothesis had the right mechanism but the wrong culprit.** You spotted the flipped Z in `#51 = IFCDIRECTION((0.,0.,-1.))`, and that is the cause — but our handling of it is spec-correct. Per IFC, the derived Y axis is Z × X, so `(0,0,-1) × (1,0,0) = (0,-1,0)`. Your profile point `(1.524, 1.524)` therefore maps to world `(1.524, -1.524)`: because you baked absolute coordinates into the profile *and* flipped the local Z, the footprint gets mirrored about the world X axis. The file is asking for a mirrored slab, and any conforming viewer will put it where we put it. That's also why your walls round-trip perfectly — they keep Z at `(0,0,1)` and carry position in the placement instead of the profile.

Your offered variant with local Z unflipped would confirm this in one round trip, and I'd genuinely like to see it — partly to close the loop, partly because it's a useful fixture for us either way.

Read through `wiki/architecture/capture-runtime.md` — here's my answer to the seam question.

**They're two different payloads, and this tool ultimately wants both — but for *this* hand-off, build JSON is the right seam.**

What A3 Atlas sends through `/import?src=` is not capture data: it's the **interpreted scene** — walls, openings, fixtures, measured materials — already converted to Pascal's graph on the scanner side, the same shape Save/Load Build round-trips. The whole point of the hand-off is that the recipient lands in an *editable* scene: repaint a wall, move a cabinet, keep working. A capture-protocol manifest can't carry that without becoming a second scene graph — which capture-runtime.md rules out in its first sentence ("not a second scene graph"). Forcing the interpreted graph through the manifest would either lose editability or bloat the protocol with scene semantics it was designed to stay out of.

The capture protocol is the right seam for the **evidence**: the RoomPlan mesh, the camera track (device motion), the scan video, a point cloud. Atlas already produces those artifacts, and the natural integration is exactly the one the doc describes — the exported build JSON later carries a `scan` node whose `captureSession` locator points at an Atlas-hosted manifest, so the editable graph and the raw capture each ride the seam they were designed for. Nothing about `/import` blocks that; the manifest URL just becomes part of the same file when we get there.

So my read: `/import` isn't a second *scene* entry point competing with capture — it's the missing HTTP entry for the object the editor already imports via the file picker. Happy to sketch the scan-node + manifest step as a follow-up issue if that helps settle where it sits.

That settles it — and it's the right answer. The distinction you drew is the one the doc was written to protect: the manifest carries evidence, never a second scene graph, and what Atlas hands off here is the interpreted scene — the same object the file picker already imports. `/import` as the missing HTTP entry for that object, with the capture manifest arriving later as a `scan` node's `captureSession` locator in the same file, is exactly where I wanted the seam to sit. Yes to the follow-up issue: sketch the scan-node + manifest step there and reference this thread.

Design decision, and a candidate: #736.

Between the two options #561 debated, neither survives the constraints in this issue. A typed `no_active_scene` throw breaks the `--stdio` quick start on the first `create_wall` (the store is attached, no scene is ever bound). Lazy draft binding silently creates persistent scenes the user never asked for, and not every store can create one without project context.

What #736 does instead: kills the *silence* rather than the skip. `publishLiveSceneSnapshot` returns `'published' | 'unbound' | 'events_unsupported'` (split on the existing `canAppendSceneEvents` seam), and all 17 mutating tool sites surface a `persistence: { status, warning }` field in their result when the change stayed in-memory — declared in each tool's output schema so structured-content validation keeps it. An AI caller reads the warning and binds a scene with `save_scene`/`load_scene`; a human reading the transcript sees exactly why nothing persisted, in the layer where they were looking.

`InMemorySceneStore` gained `appendSceneEvent`/`listSceneEvents`, so all three paths are covered by tests through a real client/server pair.

Lazy binding can still happen later as an opt-in (a `--scene new` flag on `pascal-mcp` would be the honest version of it) — but the reporting layer had to exist first either way.

Validated the branch against our real external Next.js 16.2.9 / Webpack integration.

A/B on the same consumer, with no `resolve.fallback`:

* base `67ea40efdf4a03f5897005def56e45189f2c1b69` reproduces the original `node:module` / `UnhandledSchemeError` through `manifold-3d`;
* candidate `58edd0c059991fbebdf597c878d06d53ab79edb0` completes the Webpack compilation stage (`Compiled with warnings`) with neither `node:module` nor `UnhandledSchemeError`;
* the emitted browser worker chunk is 4,696 bytes, while the exact `manifold.js` glue in the same candidate graph is 74,762 bytes; the emitted worker contains no `node:module`, so the Manifold payload is no longer bundled into it.

So #735 fixes the external-consumer bundler issue we reported, with zero webpack fallback/config on our side.

One separate caveat: our current production fork carries additional BuildBook-specific `ViewerStage` APIs that are not present upstream. After Webpack succeeds, our full Next build currently stops later during TypeScript on that fork/API parity. That is independent of the Manifold packaging fix.

CI ran the new smoke phases on `macos-latest` in ~2 min:

```
Staged Pascal web runtime 1.0.0-beta.1 at .../packages/cli/build/runtime
Archived 3309 entries to .../pascal-web-runtime-1.0.0-beta.1.tar.gz (43.16 MB)
MCP-only mode exposed 46 tools and stored a scene with no web runtime installed.
Tampered archive rejected: The Pascal web runtime archive does not match the digest published with this CLI.
Editor installed from pascal-web-runtime-1.0.0-beta.1.tar.gz on port 49487, MCP on port 49490, and a scene round-tripped between MCP and the CLI.
Packed CLI smoke passed (0.5 MB compressed, 2.5 MB unpacked, 68 files).
```

Two notes on the archive size. CI produced **43.2 MB / 3309 entries** where my local run produced **64.2 MB / 3312 entries** — the difference is what the standalone Next build traced out of each machine's `node_modules` (a full local install hoists more than `--frozen-lockfile` does), so the 64.2 MB figure in the description is the pessimistic one and real headroom under the 70 MB budget is larger than it looks.

That also means the digest is reproducible for a given tree on a given machine, not across machines. It does not need to be: `stage-runtime` writes the archive and `dist/runtime-source.json` in the same job that publishes, so the embedded digest always describes the asset that job uploads.

## What this PR does

This is a test-only change to `packages/nodes`: the suite now runs in a single bun process on virtual time instead of 13 child processes on real sleeps, and the 45 lifecycle JSON goldens become an explicit contract test. The diff is 4 added files, 23 modified, 51 removed (49 fixture files, one snapshot, one probe-spawning test), no product code. Three files that installed process-global `mock.module` mocks are fixed at the source (`wall/rectangle-tool-sfx`, `shared/roof-surface-placement-guides`, `duct-fitting/parametrics`), which is what let the `PASCAL_*_ISOLATED` re-spawn gates go away; the per-file mounted-scene setup collapses into `harness.tsx`, whose `settle()`/`advance()` run on bun's fake timers. Per the description the suite goes 173 s to 62 s at 5,098 pass / 1 skip, and the pass count rises because the ~1,370 cases that used to run inside children now count at top level.

## What this PR does

It adds a way for agents (and people) to build objects that Pascal's node recipes can't express, by writing a plain three.js module. A new package, `@pascal-app/geometry-script`, runs that module and compiles it to a GLB plus a manifest read from naming conventions (`slot_<id>` materials, `part:<id>` groups, lights, `cutout`, `anchor:<id>`, `collider`, animation clips). The result is stored content-addressed as `artifact://<sha256>` and lands in the scene as an ordinary `item` carrying its script source, so paint, hosting, the move tool, collections, bake and export keep working on it. On top of that it wires two agent tools (`author_object`, `find_by_type`), lets `place_item` target an item so things rest on or hang from authored geometry, and adds inspector controls for a script's declared params and clips.

## 1. Inventory: who owns which strings

## 2. Proposed contract

### 2.1 Keys and English as the built-in fallback
- Every user-facing string gets a key, and **the English literal stays in the code as the default**: `t('editor.buildPanel.rooms.title', 'Rooms')`. With no locale registered, behaviour and screenshots are identical to today — zero risk for English, and migration can go one surface at a time.
- Namespaces follow ownership: `editor.*`, `viewer.*`, `core.*`, `node.<kind>.*`, `plugin.<pluginId>.*`.
- Node definitions keep `presentation.label` / `description` in English; display goes through `t(\`node.${kind}.label\`, def.presentation.label)`. No node definition has to change shape.

### 2.2 Registration (no framework required in core)
- `core` exposes a tiny registry: `registerMessages(locale, namespace, messages)` and `setLocale(locale)`; `editor` exposes `useTranslate()` reading it (re-render on locale change).
- **Host app**: calls `registerMessages('pt-BR', 'editor', ptBrEditor)` before mounting `<Editor>` — exactly how it already calls `registerNode`.
- **Plugins**: a plugin manifest may carry `translations: { [locale]: messages }` for its own `plugin.<id>.*` / `node.<kind>.*` namespaces, registered when the plugin loads. Nothing in core packages is touched.
- Locale packs for core namespaces can live outside the repo (npm `@scope/pascal-locale-xx`) or in-repo later; the contract does not care.

### 2.3 Fallback
`pt-BR` → `pt` → English literal in code. Missing keys never throw and never show the key; a dev-only warning lists them.

### 2.4 Names saved into scene data
Today both patterns exist:
- **display-time** default: `getDefaultLevelName()` — "a name the user gave wins", otherwise computed when shown. Safe to translate.
- **write-time** default: e.g. `liquid-line/tool.tsx` creates nodes with `name: 'Liquid Line'`, which is persisted. Translating that literal would store the creator's language in the scene and in exports.

Proposal: default names become display-time (store no name, or a key), following the level-name pattern. Out of scope for the first PRs, but the contract should state it so nobody "translates" write-time names.

### 2.5 Server rendering and hydration
If the locale is only known in the browser, server HTML (English) and the first client render (translated) differ and React throws *Hydration failed* — the prototype hit this on the first try. The hook therefore returns the English fallback for the server snapshot (`useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getVersion, () => SERVER)`) and re-renders with the client locale right after hydration. Hosts that know the locale on the server (cookie/header) can call `setLocale` there too and skip the flash.

### 2.6 Out of scope on purpose
Exported names (GLB/IFC), agent/MCP text, catalog/material content, dev errors.

## 3. Prototype

Two commits on top of `main` @ `89e1442f`: (1) `core/src/i18n` registry (88 lines, no dependency) + `useTranslate()` hook (21 lines) + tests, and the Build panel's Rooms section and "Advanced" header moved to 16 keys (`build-panel.tsx` +20/−6); (2) a host file registering pt-BR (+32 lines, outside core). With no locale (or `?lang=en`) every string is the original English; with pt-BR the section is translated, including the caption that follows the armed shape. No translated text lives in core packages.

## 4. Suggested rollout
1. Registry + `useTranslate()` + fallback in `core`/`editor`, no strings migrated (one small PR).
2. **A CI guard in the same PR or right after:** flag new user-facing literals that bypass `t()` (JSX text, `label`/`title`/`aria-label` props, node definition labels). Without it the migration never finishes: between 1.0.2 (2026-09-18) and `main` (2026-10-02) the UI gained **612 new unique strings in 14 days** (~300/week, mostly `editor` and `nodes`). Our AST scan already does this detection and could be the starting point; it can start as a warning and only cover migrated surfaces.
3. One surface per PR from current `main`: `viewer` (38 strings) → `editor` build panel → inspectors per node kind.
4. Plugin manifest `translations` once a first plugin wants it.

The scan script and the full per-string CSV are available if useful, and the prototype can be opened as a draft PR from current `main`.

What we (Kliv, Brazil — pt-BR) can commit to once the contract is agreed: the registry PR (steps 1–2), the migration of two or three surfaces as reference (starting with `viewer` and the build panel), and the pt-BR locale pack, kept up to date as new keys land. We don't expect to migrate every surface ourselves.

## What this PR does

## Summary

Three stability fixes in the editor package, all in `packages/editor/src/components`. The biggest one is in `DragBoundingBox`: it used to build a fresh `BoxGeometry`/`PlaneGeometry` and new materials whenever the dragged dimensions or colour changed, and dispose the previous ones in an effect cleanup. That is once per frame during a resize drag, so WebGPU could still be executing a command buffer pointing at buffers that had just been freed. The new version creates one unit edge geometry and one unit ground plane at module scope, caches materials in a `Map` keyed by colour, and moves the per-frame change into the mesh transform via `position` and `scale`. The other two changes are the same small fix applied in two places: the guide-image upload `catch` blocks in `LevelReferences` and `UploadButton` discarded the caught error, so a secure-context failure showed up as a generic "Could not add that guide image." They now log the error and append its message to the toast when there is one.

## What this changes

Nodes with `bake: 'replace'` have their baked mesh hidden by `GlbScene` and get re-rendered live through their `bakeReplaceRenderer`, which until now only received `{ nodes }`. Since the baked viewer never loads the scene graph into `useScene`, a renderer that builds from other nodes (a ground surface reading its parent site's polygon) found nothing and drew an empty group. This PR threads an optional `resolve` prop, with the same signature as `GeometryContext.resolve`, from `GlbScene` down through `GlbReplaceInstances` to every replace renderer. `GlbScene` builds it from a new optional `sceneNodes` prop, memoized so the memoized `GlbReplaceInstances` subtree keeps short-circuiting on camera moves. Nothing in this repo passes `sceneNodes` yet; per the description, the plugin and the hosted viewer land after this one.

### Blocker 3: Alt-Key Misused as Snap and Alignment Bypass in Fence Drafting

- **Where**: `packages/nodes/src/fence/tool.tsx:738, 791, 821, 854, 1204`
- **Offending Code**:

- **Rule Violated**: `DECISIONS.md` **E-004** (*"Snapping is a visible per-context mode. Shift tap cycles the mode; Alt hold forces the raw cursor past snapping and collisions. This is a bundle PR: it brings four already-reviewed branches into a single merge against `main` so nothing has to be rebased against the others. #1007 is the bulk of it, moving the MCP's write tools onto one set of contracts in `@pascal-app/core/agent-tools` backed by one operation each in core, so the hosted chat and the MCP expose the same tool names, inputs and refusals (`add_wall`, `add_level`, `place_items`, `create_stair`, the room and floor tools). On top of that sit `view_scene` for agent-side rendering (#1010), the by-hand floor-item fit warning in the editor HUD and item panel (#1013), and the door leaf and style fixes with the `Style` row and `[O]`/`[L]` chips (#1009, which also renames `getDoorStyleOverrides` to `doorStyleLook`). The diff is 169 files, and the shape of it is roughly "new code in `packages/core`, deletions in `packages/mcp/src/tools`": the MCP's own `create_wall`, `create_level`, `place_item` and `cut_opening` files go away and the remaining MCP tool modules shrink to adapters. The description also notes it must land as a merge commit, because pascalorg/private-editor's bundle pins its submodule to this branch's head.

## What this PR does

A fix pass across four areas of the editor: rooms and level duplication, open wall ends, scripted (AI-authored) objects, and the 3D camera. The largest new piece is open wall end detection: `room-graph.ts` and `wall-topology.ts` gain logic to find wall ends that look joined but aren't (gap, overshoot, parallel), plus a plan to square them back up, surfaced in 2D and 3D with markers, a gap label and a one-click "Join walls" that undoes in one step. `verify_scene` reports those ends as `wall_open_end`. Level duplication now regenerates derived floor plates instead of copying them and names copies by position, so the result reads like an added level. Scripted objects get library material matching after a build, per-row and whole-group parameter resets, and reuse metadata (description, category, tags, parent script hash) plus thumbnail/floor-plan image refs that travel with the build and survive undo. The camera gains a floor-aware orbit: a downward raycast against the level's walkable surface stops the camera 0.45 m above it and pitches the view up instead of going through the floor.

Engine side of the Architect's lot work, in three parts. With a property line on the site, the terrain now renders as a block: the ground surface is masked to the parcel per fragment, and a skirt follows the property line down to one flat base, so the lot reads as a solid sitting inside mapped 3D surroundings instead of a disc that caps it. The viewer gets a `claimSceneGround(scene)` escape hatch so a map layer living outside React can take ownership of the scene ground, and the camera unlocks to 1500 m while that is the case. Separately, the site-plan setback code now carries a front or street role across an edge that continues nearly straight on (≤ 8°), which fixes the curved arc that appeared when a county parcel split one frontage into two almost-collinear lines.

Thank you for this, @luisalrp. It was the right instinct, and it took a while on our side to settle what a published image should look like. Closing it now because the image is live, through a broader change that went further than a bootstrap workflow: #1032 (with #1038, #1049 and #1050 for the release plumbing).

What shipped, and why it needed more than publishing:

- **Official image.** `ghcr.io/pascalorg/pascal-editor`, tagged with the npm version (`1.0.4` today) plus `latest` / `beta`, linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, published by the same release workflow as the packages so a release's container and its CLI runtime are the same bits. Built per architecture on native runners and stitched into one manifest. Compose now pulls the image; `docker compose build` still builds from a checkout.
- **Public URL at runtime.** The app used to inline `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL` at build time, so one image could serve one domain. The server pages now read the store directly instead of fetching their own API, and `PASCAL_PUBLIC_URL` is read per request. One image serves any domain or port.
- **Authentication.** A self-hosted instance had none. `PASCAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD` now gates every page and the scene API behind `/login`; agents keep the bearer token; a network host with nothing configured serves a setup page and nothing else; `PASCAL_AUTH=proxy` defers to an authenticating reverse proxy. Loopback and the CLI's managed editor stay open.
- **A product, not a shell.** Home at `/` lists projects with thumbnails (now actually stored), rename and delete; the editor has a navbar; `/settings` shows the instance and the agent endpoint; projects can be shared as read-only embeds.

Two details from this PR made it in, in spirit: the `.dockerignore` exclusion of `*.tsbuildinfo` (which bit us for real in #1038) and the OCI source metadata on the image.

Thanks @Aymericr. Here is a short design note for the four points, building on @luis-caf's proposal (happy for @luis-caf to fold it into theirs or take the registry PR as planned).

**1. Host-registered packs, no core edits**
- `core` gets a small registry: `registerMessages(locale, namespace, messages)`, `setLocale(locale)`, `getLocale()`, `subscribe(listener)`. No dependency.
- Namespaces follow ownership: `editor.*`, `viewer.*`, `core.*`, `node.<kind>.*`, `plugin.<id>.*`. A host registers packs before mounting `<Editor>`, the same way it calls `registerNode`. Later registrations for the same locale/namespace merge over earlier ones, so a host can adapt a bundled pack.
- In code, the English literal stays as the default: `t('editor.buildPanel.rooms.title', 'Rooms')`. Lookup: `pt-BR` → `pt` → the English literal. A missing key never throws and never shows the key. In development it logs a warning.

**2. Locale before the editor loads**
- An embed takes `locale` in its config (`<Editor locale="tr" />`); the standalone app and iframes take `?lang=tr`. Either one calls `setLocale` before the first render.
- A host that knows the locale on the server (cookie or header) sets it there too, so the server HTML and the first client render agree: no English flash, no hydration mismatch. Without it, the hook returns English for the server snapshot and switches right after hydration.
- `setLocale` at runtime re-renders the subscribed components, so a host can offer a language switch.

**3. Numbers and units follow the locale**
- One formatter in `core`: `formatNumber(value, { min, max })` and `formatLength(meters, unit)` on top of `Intl.NumberFormat(getLocale())`. A readout and its label then never disagree (`2,75 m` in tr and pl, `2.75 m` in en).
- The unit system (m / cm / mm, m²) is a separate setting from the language. Inputs accept the locale's decimal separator as well as `.`.

**4. Scene data stays language-neutral**
- Translation changes only what is rendered. Nothing in a scene, an export (GLB/IFC) or an MCP/agent result is translated.
- Default names are computed when shown, following the `getDefaultLevelName()` pattern. A node stores a name only when a person gives one. Write-time defaults such as `name: 'Liquid Line'` move to display time surface by surface. Until a surface has moved, it keeps writing its English default, as it does today.
- A test can guard this: build a scene under a non-English locale, serialize it, and expect it to equal the same scene built under English.

**First PR (as you suggested)**
The registry, the hook, the fallback and the number formatter, with the `viewer` strings (~38) converted, plus screenshots in a second language. #1022 rebases onto it. A CI check that flags new user-facing literals bypassing `t()` can follow as a warning on converted surfaces.

From our side (Forehome, `tr`): we can test the registry against a real downstream host that switches language at runtime and renders on the server, and we will maintain the `tr` pack.

Thanks @Aymericr! I addressed all three points in e40f704:

1. **Consistent `recipe` access (`check-collisions.ts`)**: Dropped the redundant `?.` on `node.recipe.name` since `ProceduralItemNode` always validates a required `recipe`, matching `node.recipe.name` in `source.assetId` and `node.asset.name` for catalog items.
2. **Wall-hosted procedural skip reason**: Split out the `node.type === 'procedural-item' && node.wallId` check ahead of the generic non-level parent check so wall-hosted procedural items report `unsupported_attachment` in both `floorOnly: true` and `floorOnly: false` modes, and added a regression assertion for both modes in `check-collisions.test.ts`.
3. **Why `furniture-kind.ts` is included**: Once floor-standing `procedural-item` nodes enter `collectOccupiedFootprints` and `findItemItemCollisions`, `layoutIssuesFromScene` needs `isFloorUnderlay` and `designedTogether` / `pairRole` to recognize `ProceduralItemNode` as well; otherwise procedural rugs and intentionally paired procedural furniture (like dining chairs near tables) trigger false-positive `item_overlap` or `item_too_close` findings in `verify_scene`. (I noted this in the second bullet of the PR description as well.)

Thanks @Aymericr! I addressed all four points in cd93aaa and updated the PR description:

1. **Public `CameraSchema` change & schema test**: Called out the `CameraSchema.mode` change (`.default('perspective')` -> `.optional()`) in the PR description for `@pascal-app/core` consumers and MCP clients, and added `packages/core/src/schema/camera.test.ts` verifying that legacy `{ position, target }` cameras parse with `mode: undefined` and round-trip cleanly through JSON serialization and `SiteNode.parse`.
